title: Psychological attachment styles and post-treatment outcomes following therapy for oral squamous cell carcinoma: a multicenter observational study
summary:
Psychological and social factors influence how people cope with illness, follow medical advice, and maintain their health over the long term. This relationship has already been studied in the context of chronic inflammatory diseases such as periodontitis. However, there have been few studies to date on people who have been treated for oral cancer (oral squamous cell carcinoma, OSCC).
The treatment of oral cancer can have a significant impact on daily life. Surgery and additional therapies such as radiation or chemotherapy can alter speech, swallowing, facial expressions, and physical appearance. As a result, many patients suffer from functional and aesthetic limitations, which are often associated with psychological distress.

These changes can lead patients to withdraw socially, feel stigmatized, or suffer from anxiety and depressive symptoms. In particular, the fear of a recurrence of the disease continues to weigh heavily on many patients long after the actual cancer treatment has ended. Studies show that these psychological burdens significantly impair quality of life and can also influence health behaviors.

Follow-up care after OSCC treatment requires active cooperation from patients. This includes regular checkups, careful oral hygiene, changing unhealthy habits, and promptly addressing any potential symptoms. How well people cope with this may also depend on how they manage stress, regulate their emotions, and build trust with others.

An important psychological factor here is what is known as attachment behavior. People with insecure attachment styles are more likely to have difficulty coping with stress, use ineffective coping strategies, and often adhere less consistently to medical recommendations. Furthermore, there is evidence that psychological stress can also influence physical inflammatory responses.

Therefore, it stands to reason that attachment patterns could also play a role in patients following OSCC surgery. However, this connection has hardly been investigated to date. The aim of the study is therefore to investigate this potential influence in greater detail.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Adult patients from the age of 18 and older
OSCC surgery performed ≥1 year prior to study enrollment
Written informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
Inability to give consent
Lack of follow-up data
